extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in essays, moral/philosophical reflections, and medical skepticism (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: A first‑person early‑modern essay reflecting skeptically on physicians, remedies, baths, and medical custom, using anecdotes, classical references, and rhetorical irony. The piece mixes practical advice, epistemic critique of medical evidence, and personal disposition toward health and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and depth of physician's required knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: He had need of too many parts, considerations, and circumstances, rightly to level his design: he must know the sick person’s complexion, his temperament, his humours, inclinations, actions, nay, his very thoughts and imaginations; he must be assured of the external circumstances, of the nature of the place, the quality of the air and season, the situation of the planets, and their influences: he must know in the disease, the causes, prognostics, affections, and critical days; in the drugs, the weight, the power of working, the country, figure, age, and dispensation...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a criterion for judging a physician's competence: the author argues that the sheer number of required considerations makes reliable medical judgment almost impossible and explains why errors are common (e.g., disputes over urine interpretation, divergent opinions). Treat claims of exhaustive knowledge with skepticism; expect unavoidable uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgery regarded as more certain than physic
rubrics_metrics.description: I conclude surgery to be much more certain, by reason that it sees and feels what it does, and so goes less upon conjecture; whereas the physicians have no ‘speculum matricis’, by which to examine our brains, lungs, and liver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interventions where the problem is palpable and observable; value empirical, visible procedures over speculative internal diagnoses. Use tangible evidence (what one sees and feels) to assess certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility of medical promises (virtues separating in mixtures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the very promises of physic are incredible in themselves... they will needs persuade us, that of their ingredients one will heat the stomach and the other will cool the liver... is it not a kind of madness to imagine or to hope that these differing virtues should separate themselves from one another in this mixture and confusion, to perform so many various errands?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about compound remedies critically: the essay warns that mixing many ingredients makes it implausible that each will perform separate, targeted operations. Watch for metaphors (tickets lost/changed) to spot fanciful claims; consider interactions, corruption of properties, and reliance on others to compound medicines as risk factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization over universal practice
rubrics_metrics.description: To each disease, to each part of the body, its particular workman; for that part was more properly and with less confusion cared for, seeing the person looked to nothing else... Ours are not aware that he who provides for all, provides for nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor specialized practitioners who focus on particular diseases or parts rather than generalists claiming competence over everything. The analogy to tailors/cooks recommends dividing tasks to improve performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and contradiction in regimen advice
rubrics_metrics.description: They have the like uniformity in the counsels they give us for the regimen of life: it is good to make water often; it is good not to make water often... it is good to have often to do with women... it is also very ill to have often to do with women... It is good to bathe frequently... it is also ill...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal consistency (or lack thereof) of medical recommendations as a test of reliability. When authorities offer contradictory prescriptions for the same condition, treat such counsels as weak evidence and beware of dogmatic adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate expectations for baths and spa cures
rubrics_metrics.description: They have not the virtue to raise men from desperate and inveterate diseases, but they may help some light indisposition, or prevent some threatening alteration... He who does not bring along with him so much cheerfulness as to enjoy the pleasure of the company... will doubtless lose the best and surest part of their effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge baths/spas as useful for mild conditions, appetite, digestion, and prevention rather than miraculous cures. Consider setting, company, lodging, and one’s mental disposition as part of the 'treatment' effect. Do not expect baths to cure entrenched disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: National and procedural variation in treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nation has particular opinions touching their use, and particular rules and methods in using them... Drinking them is not at all received in Germany; the Germans bathe for all diseases... in Italy, where they drink nine days, they bathe at least thirty... Here we are ordered to walk to digest it; there we are kept in bed after taking it...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a treatment or custom, account for cultural and procedural differences. Variation in practice across places undermines claims of universal efficacy; examine local methods and durations rather than assuming one-size-fits-all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on custom, 'quintessence', and occult properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest part, I should say above two-thirds of the medicinal virtues, consist in the quintessence or occult property of simples, of which we can have no other instruction than use and custom; for quintessence is no other than a quality of which we cannot by our reason find out the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat appeals to 'quintessence' or occult properties as non‑rational explanations dependent on tradition rather than demonstrable mechanisms. Use the provenance and historical use of simples as weak evidence; require stronger causal reasoning for robust claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward anecdotal 'experiments' and one-off cures
rubrics_metrics.description: After the cure is performed, how can he assure himself that it was not because the disease had arrived at its period or an effect of chance?... And after the rule is concluded, by whom, I pray you?... that three witnesses, three doctors, should lord it over all mankind, is against reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand replication, systematic recording, and control for confounders when accepting therapeutic claims. Beware of single examples, post hoc attributions, and small numbers of witnesses; require methodical repetition and broader testimony before accepting causal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patients' fear and impatience as causes of gullibility
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis the fear of death and of pain, impatience of disease, and a violent and indiscreet desire of a present cure, that so blind us: ‘tis pure cowardice that makes our belief so pliable and easy to be imposed upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an ethical/psychological criterion: evaluate whether a patient's decisions are driven by fear/urgency rather than evidence. Counsel restraint and patience; recognize that desperation increases vulnerability to quackery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical patient behavior and minimal compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When I am sick I send for them if they be near, only to have their company, and pay them as others do. I give them leave to command me to keep myself warm... and to appoint leeks or lettuce for my broth; and so as to all other things, which are indifferent to my palate and custom. I know very well that I do nothing for them in so doing...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As guidance for patients: consult physicians for companionship/advice but follow only reasonable, familiar, or harmless prescriptions; prioritize comfort and simple remedies over strange, harsh, or extravagant treatments. Do not assume physicians' prescriptions are necessarily superior to common‑sense remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware remedies derived from diseased sources
rubrics_metrics.description: I, hearing that the blood of a he-goat was with many in very great esteem... gave order to have a goat fed... the cook had found two or three great balls in his paunch... ’Tis likely these are stones of the same nature with ours and if so, it must needs be a very vain hope... to extract their cure from the blood of a beast that was himself about to die of the same disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the provenance of remedies: if a purported cure comes from an organism suffering the same malady, question the plausibility that it could serve as a remedy. Consider contamination and shared pathology as reasons to distrust such prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting professional opportunism and evasive tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pliny... twits them with this, that when they are at the end of their rope, they have a pretty device to save themselves, by recommending their patients... to vows and miracles... a third way of saving their own credit... which is to send us to the better air of some other country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of ritual, miraculous appeals, or evasive prescriptions (e.g., sending a patient away) as indicators a practitioner is defending reputation rather than treating effectively. Treat last‑resort recommendations that primarily protect the practitioner’s credit with suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial/ethical criterion for writing: authenticity and practical life
rubrics_metrics.description: I require nothing more of these writings, but to present me to your memory such as I naturally am... Studies, to teach me to do, and not to write. I have made it my whole business to frame my life: this has been my trade and my work; I am less a writer of books than anything else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing personal essays or moral reflections, prioritize presenting an authentic self and practical wisdom rather than crafting a reputation for posterity. Value conduct and usefulness of learning over literary vanity; prefer immediacy and candidness in tone.
